adult-use.detail: State law (AS 17.38) makes marijuana use legal only for people 21 and older. An adult may possess up to 1 ounce for personal use.
adult-use.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs (AS 17.38)

buying.detail: Marijuana may be bought only from licensed retail marijuana stores. Delivery is not allowed.
buying.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

driving.detail: It is a crime to drive while impaired by marijuana.
driving.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

employment.short: Employers may restrict employees’ marijuana use
employment.detail: Alaska’s marijuana law says nothing in it requires an employer to permit or accommodate the use, possession or growing of marijuana in the workplace, or affects an employer’s ability to have policies restricting marijuana use by employees. Employers and others who control private property may also prohibit marijuana on it. This is the Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office’s copy of the chapter as of July 25, 2018, which is marked as not an official copy.

home-grow.short: Up to 12 plants per home, 6 mature
home-grow.detail: No more than 12 plants, with six or fewer mature and flowering, may be present in a single dwelling.
home-grow.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

medical.detail: Medical cards are issued under AS 17.37. The adult-use law did not change their privileges or prohibitions.
medical.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs (AS 17.37)

possession.detail: An adult 21 or older may possess up to 1 ounce of marijuana for personal use.
possession.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

public-use.short: Not in public; some stores allow on-site use
public-use.detail: Using marijuana in public is illegal. Some licensed retail stores hold an on-site consumption endorsement that allows use there.
public-use.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

sharing.detail: An adult 21 or older may give 1 ounce or less to another adult 21 or older. Buying or selling it outside licensed stores is not allowed.
sharing.citation: Alaska Alcohol & Marijuana Control Office, Marijuana FAQs

adult-use.detail: Alabama has no adult-use law. A first offense of possessing marijuana for personal use is a Class A misdemeanor. That is existing law as summarized in a February 2026 Senate bill; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: Code of Ala. 13A-12-214, per the 2026 Senate Bill 285 synopsis; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

medical.detail: The Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission runs the state’s medical cannabis program for patients and caregivers. Whether licensed dispensaries are open is not yet reviewed.
medical.citation: Alabama Medical Cannabis Commission

adult-use.detail: Arkansas has no adult-use law. Possessing less than 4 ounces of marijuana is a Class A misdemeanor. That is the law as the Arkansas Sentencing Commission quoted it in 2019; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: Ark. Code 5-64-419(b)(5)(A), per the Arkansas Sentencing Commission (2019); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Arkansas’s constitution as barring employers from discriminating against qualifying patients and caregivers in hiring, firing or the terms of employment. Its chart says the amendment still lets employers take listed actions and points to the amendment for the full limits. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: Ark. Const. amend. 98, § 3, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

medical.detail: The Arkansas Department of Health issues medical marijuana registry cards. A separate state agency licenses dispensaries.
medical.citation: Arkansas Department of Health, Medical marijuana

adult-use.detail: An adult 21 or older may possess and use 1 ounce or less of marijuana, of which no more than 5 grams may be concentrate.

buying.detail: Licensed marijuana establishments may sell to consumers, up to 1 ounce per transaction, no more than 5 grams of it concentrate.

driving.short: No driving impaired to the slightest degree
driving.detail: The law does not allow driving while impaired to even the slightest degree by marijuana, or consuming it while driving or riding in a vehicle. Metabolites in a driver’s system count toward an impaired-driving charge only if the driver is impaired to the slightest degree.

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Arizona as barring employers from refusing to hire, firing or penalizing a registered patient for that status or for a positive marijuana test, unless the person used or was impaired by marijuana at work. Its chart lists an exception where the employer would lose a federal benefit. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: A.R.S. § 36-2813, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.detail: Plants must be at the adult’s primary residence, in an enclosed area with a lock that keeps out minors and not visible from public view. No more than 12 plants at a residence with two or more adults.

medical.detail: The Arizona Department of Health Services licenses the medical marijuana program for qualifying patients, caregivers and dispensaries.
medical.citation: Arizona Department of Health Services, Marijuana licensing

possession.detail: No more than 5 grams of the 1 ounce may be marijuana concentrate.

public-use.short: No smoking in public places or open spaces
public-use.detail: Smoking marijuana in a public place or open space is not allowed and is a petty offense. Consuming it while driving or riding in a vehicle is also not allowed.

record-relief.short: 2.5 ounces or less, six plants or paraphernalia
record-relief.detail: Arizona’s courts say Proposition 207 added A.R.S. § 36-2862, which lets some people petition a court for an order sealing their marijuana-related criminal records; the courts’ forms call this expungement. It covers a person arrested, charged, convicted or acquitted, for conduct before November 30, 2020, of possessing, consuming or transporting 2.5 ounces or less of marijuana (no more than 12.5 grams of it concentrate), of possessing, transporting, growing or processing up to six plants at a primary residence for personal use, or of a marijuana paraphernalia offense. Courts have taken petitions since July 12, 2021 and may not charge a filing fee. The petition goes to the court that resolved the case or, if no case was filed, to the Superior Court in the county of the arrest. A prosecuting agency may also file.
record-relief.citation: A.R.S. § 36-2862, per the Arizona Judicial Branch’s Prop 207 page, petition instructions and court staff presentation

sharing.short: Up to 1 ounce or 6 plants, free
sharing.detail: An adult may transfer 1 ounce or less, or up to six plants, to another adult 21 or older without payment and without advertising or promoting it.

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy cannabis for adult use.
adult-use.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

buying.detail: Every cannabis retailer must hold a Department of Cannabis Control license. The department’s license search finds licensed retailers.
buying.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

driving.detail: Having an open container of cannabis while driving or riding in a vehicle is illegal. Cannabis in a vehicle must be in a sealed package or container, or in the trunk. Officers can pull a driver over for a sobriety test if they suspect the driver is under the influence of cannabis.
driving.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

employment.detail: Since January 1, 2024, California employers generally cannot refuse to hire, fire or penalize someone for using cannabis off the job and away from the workplace, or because a drug test finds only non-psychoactive cannabis metabolites. Employers may still act on a scientifically valid test for psychoactive THC, keep a drug-free workplace and bar use, possession or impairment on the job. The protections do not cover employers with four or fewer employees, jobs that need a federal background investigation or security clearance, or employees in the building and construction trades.
employment.citation: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954, per the Civil Rights Department’s FAQ (January 2024)

home-grow.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to six cannabis plants at home.
home-grow.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

medical.detail: People 18 and older with a physician’s recommendation may buy for medicinal use, and medicinal users have higher possession limits.
medical.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

possession.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 28.5 grams of cannabis and up to 8 grams of concentrated cannabis.
possession.citation: Judicial Council of California, Proposition 64: The Adult Use of Marijuana Act

public-use.short: Not in public; private property only
public-use.detail: Cannabis may be used on private property, but not in public places such as restaurants or bars.
public-use.citation: California Department of Cannabis Control, What’s legal

record-relief.detail: California’s courts say the state reviews records itself: under a 2019 law the Department of Justice identified cases that might qualify under Proposition 64, and a 2023 law required courts to grant relief by March 1, 2023 in cases prosecutors had not challenged. A person can also apply. Someone who has completed a sentence may ask the trial court to dismiss and seal an eligible conviction, or to redesignate it as a misdemeanor or infraction; someone still serving a sentence may petition for resentencing or dismissal.
record-relief.citation: Cal. Health & Safety Code §§ 11361.8 and 11361.9, per the Judicial Branch of California’s Proposition 64 page

sharing.detail: Adults may give away up to 28.5 grams of cannabis and 8 grams of concentrated cannabis to another adult 21 or older without compensation.
sharing.citation: Judicial Council of California, Proposition 64: The Adult Use of Marijuana Act

adult-use.detail: It is illegal for anyone under 21 to buy, have or use retail cannabis. Adults 21 and older can have up to 2 ounces.
adult-use.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

buying.short: Licensed stores, 1 ounce at a time
buying.detail: Buy retail cannabis only from licensed retail stores, up to 1 ounce at a time, with valid ID showing you are 21 or older.
buying.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

driving.detail: A driver affected to the slightest degree can be arrested for DUI or DWAI. A blood test of 5 nanograms or more of active THC per milliliter lets a court assume the driver was under the influence. Neither drivers nor passengers may open cannabis packaging and use the product in a vehicle, even when it is not moving.
driving.citation: State of Colorado, Driving and traveling

employment.short: Employers may act on a THC drug test
employment.detail: Colorado’s cannabis site says that even though cannabis is legal, employers can still test for THC and make employment decisions based on the results. It advises people to learn their workplace’s policies before using cannabis.
employment.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use, “Drug testing at work”

home-grow.detail: Each Colorado resident 21 or older may grow up to six plants, with up to three flowering at a time, in an enclosed, locked area that cannot be viewed openly. Local laws can be stricter; Denver caps a home at 12 plants.
home-grow.citation: State of Colorado, Home grow laws

medical.detail: Colorado’s state site says medical cannabis has its own use and possession rules. DISA’s national map also lists medical use as legal.
medical.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use; DISA national map

possession.detail: Adults 21 and older can have up to 2 ounces. Having more can bring charges and fines.
possession.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

public-use.detail: Use is not allowed in public places such as sidewalks, parks and restaurants, or on federal land, including national parks and forests.
public-use.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

record-relief.short: Many drug offenses; motion for now-legal conduct
record-relief.detail: Colorado’s courts publish a no-fee motion to seal a conviction for conduct that state law no longer prohibits (forms JDF 2370, 2371 and 2374, under C.R.S. § 24-72-711): it is filed in the criminal case once the sentence and any supervision are complete, with a copy to the prosecutor, needs no criminal history report, and agencies generally seal within 30 days of the order. The forms do not name marijuana. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists a separate Clean Slate law that seals many drug misdemeanors and felonies after waiting periods, automatically from 2024, and 2020 pardons for possession of up to two ounces; those points are not yet checked against the state’s own law.
record-relief.citation: C.R.S. § 24-72-711, per the Colorado Judicial Branch’s forms JDF 2370 and JDF 2374 (July 1, 2025); Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

sharing.detail: Adults may give up to 2 ounces to another adult 21 or older but may not sell cannabis, including homegrown cannabis.
sharing.citation: State of Colorado, Laws about cannabis use

adult-use.detail: The state’s adult-use page says residents over 21 can legally possess and consume cannabis, and that possessing 1.5 ounces is legal.
adult-use.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Adult-use cannabis in Connecticut

buying.detail: Adult-use sales have started at licensed retailers.
buying.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Adult-use cannabis in Connecticut

driving.detail: Driving under the influence of cannabis is a criminal offense with the same penalties as an alcohol DUI. Connecticut sets no THC blood level; trained officers assess impairment.
driving.citation: Connecticut Department of Transportation Highway Safety Office, Driving high

employment.short: Unless an employer policy bars it
employment.detail: Since July 1, 2022, an employer that is not exempt may not prohibit cannabis use outside work, or act on a positive THC test, unless it has adopted a policy that says otherwise. Exempt employers may regulate off-duty use as they could before the law. Employers generally may not act on cannabis use from before a person applied or was hired. The state’s cannabis site says an employer cannot require a medical marijuana patient to refrain from off-duty use.
employment.citation: State of Connecticut, Adult-Use Cannabis in Connecticut, workplace questions (2021 and 2023)

home-grow.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to three mature and three immature plants at their primary residence, with a cap of 12 plants per household. Plants must be indoors, not visible from the street and out of reach of anyone under 21.
home-grow.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Can I grow cannabis at home?

medical.detail: Connecticut’s medical marijuana program continues to serve patients alongside adult use.
medical.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Adult-use cannabis in Connecticut

possession.detail: The state’s adult-use page says possessing 1.5 ounces of cannabis is legal.
possession.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Adult-use cannabis in Connecticut

public-use.short: Local rules; banned in state parks
public-use.detail: You generally cannot smoke or vape cannabis anywhere tobacco smoking or vaping is banned. Cities and towns may regulate public consumption, and use is prohibited in state parks, on state beaches and on state waters.
public-use.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Where can I use cannabis?

record-relief.short: Some possession convictions; others by petition
record-relief.detail: Connecticut’s Clean Slate site says convictions under General Statutes § 21a-279(c) imposed from January 1, 2000 through September 30, 2015 were set to be erased automatically on January 1, 2023, with nothing for the person to do. Others need a petition to the court, accepted since July 1, 2022: possession of four ounces or less under § 21a-279 imposed before January 1, 2000 or from October 1, 2015 through June 30, 2021; cannabis paraphernalia under § 21a-267(a) imposed before July 1, 2021; and making, selling or giving four ounces or less, or six plants grown at home for personal use, under § 21a-277(b) imposed before July 1, 2021. There is no official petition form; the court either erases the conviction without a hearing or schedules one.
record-relief.citation: Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 54-142d and 54-142v, per the State of Connecticut’s Clean Slate pages on cannabis erasure

sharing.short: Free gifts in a bona fide social relationship
sharing.detail: People with a bona fide social relationship may give each other cannabis without payment or exchange and not tied to a sale. Gifts tied to donations, paid-entry locations or event giveaways are prohibited, and medical marijuana may not be gifted.
sharing.citation: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, Can I gift cannabis to other individuals?

adult-use.detail: A person at least 21 may possess 2 ounces or less and use marijuana on private property.
adult-use.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

buying.detail: DC police guidance says selling any amount of marijuana to another person is illegal. Licensed medical cannabis retailers serve registered patients.
buying.citation: Metropolitan Police Department; DC Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration

driving.detail: Operating a vehicle or boat under the influence of marijuana is an arrestable offense, and consuming marijuana in a vehicle in public space is a violation.
driving.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

employment.detail: An employer may not refuse to hire, fire, suspend, demote, fail to promote or penalize someone for using cannabis, for being a medical cannabis patient, or for cannabinoid metabolites in a drug test without other signs of impairment. Employers may act when the job is designated safety-sensitive, when federal law, a federal contract or funding requires it, when cannabis is used or possessed at work, or when the employee is impaired at work. They may still test after an accident or on reasonable suspicion. The act took effect on October 22, 2022; its protections applied no earlier than 365 days after the Mayor approved it.
employment.citation: D.C. Law 24-190, Cannabis Employment Protections Amendment Act of 2022, section 102

home-grow.detail: An adult may cultivate up to six plants within their residence, no more than three of them mature.
home-grow.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

medical.detail: DC’s Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration registers medical cannabis patients and caregivers and licenses medical cannabis retailers.
medical.citation: DC Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration

possession.detail: A person at least 21 may possess 2 ounces or less.
possession.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

public-use.detail: Use is prohibited on any street, sidewalk, alley, park or parking area. Using medical marijuana in public is also a criminal offense.
public-use.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

record-relief.detail: D.C. Code § 16-802 directs the Superior Court to order automatic expungement of records related only to an offense that was later decriminalized or legalized, and of records related only to simple possession of any quantity of marijuana before February 15, 2015, once the case has ended and unless the prosecutor shows that the record should be kept or that the person does not qualify. Eligible records are to be expunged by October 1, 2027, or within 90 days after the case ends, whichever is later. Under the same 2022 law a person granted expungement cannot be held guilty of perjury for not disclosing the record. The Code’s notes give March 1, 2025 as the date the section began to apply, though several notes on the page conflict.
record-relief.citation: D.C. Code § 16-802 (Second Chance Amendment Act of 2022, D.C. Law 24-284)

sharing.detail: An adult may transfer 1 ounce or less to another person 21 or older when no payment or exchange of goods or services is involved.
sharing.citation: Metropolitan Police Department, The facts on DC marijuana laws

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and over may possess up to 1 ounce of marijuana or 750 milligrams of concentrated THC products.
adult-use.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Adult use

buying.detail: Adult-use sales began August 1, 2025. Adults 21 and older may buy from licensed cannabis retailers; the state says only purchases from licensed retailers are legal.
buying.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, sales launch announcement (August 1, 2025)

driving.detail: The Office of the Marijuana Commissioner says driving under the influence is still illegal.
driving.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Adult use

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Delaware as barring employers from discriminating against a cardholder for that status or for a positive marijuana test, unless the person used, possessed or was impaired by marijuana at work. Its chart lists an exception where the employer would lose a federal monetary or licensing benefit. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: 16 Del. C. § 4905A, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.detail: Home cultivation remains prohibited.
home-grow.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Adult use

medical.detail: Medical marijuana may be authorized by a doctor to relieve symptoms of certain diseases.
medical.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner

possession.detail: Adults 21 and over may possess up to 1 ounce of marijuana or 750 milligrams of concentrated THC products.
possession.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Adult use

public-use.detail: Public consumption remains prohibited.
public-use.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Adult use

record-relief.detail: Delaware law makes a case eligible for mandatory expungement where the person was convicted of possession of marijuana or of drug paraphernalia, or both in the same case, even if the person has other convictions that cannot be expunged, as long as every other charge in the case is eligible. Since August 1, 2024 the State Bureau of Identification must identify cases eligible for mandatory expungement each month and expunge them; a person may still file a petition if that has not happened. The law is a general expungement law that covers other offenses on other terms. A person need not disclose an expunged record, and courts and police answer other inquiries that there is no record.

sharing.short: Yes, with no exchange of money
sharing.detail: Adults may share marijuana with other adults as long as no money is exchanged.
sharing.citation: Delaware Office of the Marijuana Commissioner, Frequently asked questions

adult-use.detail: Florida has no adult-use law. Possessing 20 grams of cannabis or less is a first-degree misdemeanor; larger amounts are felonies.

medical.detail: Medical marijuana and low-THC cannabis are available to qualified patients. A qualified physician orders them, and licensed medical marijuana treatment centers are the only businesses allowed to dispense them.
medical.citation: Florida Office of Medical Marijuana Use

adult-use.detail: Georgia has no adult-use law. The state’s Access to Medical Cannabis Commission says adult-use marijuana is not legal and that growing, possessing and smoking marijuana are crimes. Possessing 1 ounce or less is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 12 months in jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both.
adult-use.citation: Georgia Access to Medical Cannabis Commission FAQ; O.C.G.A. 16-13-2(b)

medical.detail: Georgia’s commission runs a medical cannabis registry and licenses dispensaries. DISA’s national map lists Georgia as CBD oil only.
medical.citation: Georgia Access to Medical Cannabis Commission; DISA national map

adult-use.detail: Hawaii has no adult-use law. Possessing 3 grams of marijuana or less is a violation with a $130 fine rather than a crime, and distribution remains illegal. That is how the Attorney General’s office described current law in February 2024; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: Haw. Rev. Stat. 712-1249(2), per Department of the Attorney General testimony (2024); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

medical.detail: Patients must register with the Department of Health before medical use. The department also runs a dispensary program that serves qualified patients.
medical.citation: Hawaii Department of Health, Medical cannabis

adult-use.detail: Iowa has no adult-use law. A first conviction for possessing marijuana can bring up to six months in jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both. Penalties rise for repeat offenses.
adult-use.citation: Iowa Code 124.401(5)

medical.detail: The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services registers patients 18 and older who have a health care practitioner’s certification, with cards good for one year. Cardholders buy from five licensed dispensaries. The program page also links a waiver form for the limit of 4.5 grams of THC per 90 days.
medical.citation: Iowa Department of Health and Human Services, Medical cannabis patients and caregivers

adult-use.detail: Idaho has no adult-use law. Possessing 3 ounces of marijuana or less is a misdemeanor, with a fine of at least $300 for anyone 18 or older. More than 3 ounces is a felony punishable by up to 5 years in prison, a fine of up to $10,000, or both.
adult-use.citation: Idaho Code 37-2732(e)

medical.detail: Idaho has no medical marijuana law. The possession penalties in Idaho Code 37-2732 make no exception for medical use.
medical.citation: Idaho Code 37-2732

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy cannabis. Residents and non-residents have different possession limits.
adult-use.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

buying.detail: 291 dispensaries were licensed to sell cannabis to adults 21 and older as of November 1, 2026.
buying.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer

driving.short: Illegal at 5 ng/ml THC in blood
driving.detail: Driving is prohibited with 5 nanograms of THC per milliliter of whole blood, or 10 nanograms in another bodily substance, within two hours of driving.
driving.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Illinois as giving limited protection: employers may not penalize someone solely for being a registered patient or caregiver, but may enforce drug-testing, zero-tolerance and drug-free workplace policies that are applied without discrimination. Its chart lists an exception for federal law or loss of a federal benefit. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: 410 ILCS 130/40 and 130/50, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.short: Registered patients only, up to 5 plants
home-grow.detail: Only registered qualifying medical cannabis patients may grow, up to five plants at home.
home-grow.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

medical.detail: Illinois registers medical cannabis patients and caregivers. 191 dispensaries were licensed to sell medical cannabis as of November 1, 2026.
medical.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer

possession.detail: Residents over 21: 60 grams of flower, 1,000 milligrams of THC in infused products and 10 grams of concentrate. Non-residents: 30 grams, 500 milligrams and 5 grams. The amounts are cumulative.
possession.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

public-use.detail: The law does not permit using cannabis in any public place, and cannabis cannot be used in a motor vehicle.
public-use.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

record-relief.short: Under 30 grams: automatic if no conviction
record-relief.detail: Illinois’s cannabis site says minor cannabis offenses that did not end in a conviction, usually possession, manufacture, delivery or intent to deliver under 30 grams, are expunged automatically and removed from the public record. Minor offenses that ended in a conviction may be pardoned by the Governor, which expunges the record, and county State’s Attorneys may ask courts to vacate and expunge convictions. The site names New Leaf Illinois, a statewide, state-funded initiative, for free legal help.
record-relief.citation: Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act, per the State of Illinois cannabis site’s Expungement page

sharing.detail: Adults may give cannabis as a purely non-commercial gift to another adult 21 or older. Medical cannabis patients may not gift their medical cannabis.
sharing.citation: Illinois Cannabis Regulation Oversight Officer, FAQs

adult-use.detail: Indiana has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a Class B misdemeanor. It is a Class A misdemeanor with a prior drug conviction, and a Level 6 felony with a prior drug conviction and 30 grams or more.
adult-use.citation: Indiana Code 35-48-4-11

medical.detail: Indiana has no medical marijuana law. Its possession statute, Indiana Code 35-48-4-11, makes no exception for medical use.
medical.citation: Indiana Code 35-48-4-11

adult-use.detail: Kansas has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a Class B nonperson misdemeanor. One prior conviction makes it a Class A misdemeanor, and two or more make it a drug felony.

medical.short: Legal defense for CBD treatment oil
medical.detail: Kansas law gives an affirmative defense to a person charged with possessing a cannabidiol treatment preparation for a debilitating medical condition who has a letter from a Kansas physician dated within the past 15 months. It is a defense in court, not a program for buying medical marijuana.

adult-use.detail: Kentucky has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a Class B misdemeanor with no more than 45 days in jail. The offense does not apply to medical cannabis cardholders.

medical.detail: Senate Bill 47 legalized medical cannabis effective January 1, 2025. The Office of Medical Cannabis runs the program.
medical.citation: Kentucky Office of Medical Cannabis

adult-use.detail: Louisiana has no adult-use law. Without medical authorization, possessing 14 grams or less brings a summons and a fine of up to $100. A first conviction for more than 14 grams can bring up to six months in jail, a $500 fine, or both.

employment.short: State employees who are medical patients
employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Louisiana as protecting state government employees only: a state employer may not penalize an employee solely for a positive marijuana test if the employee has a physician’s recommendation. Its chart lists exceptions for use or impairment at work and for safety and law-enforcement roles. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: La. R.S. 49:1016, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

medical.detail: The Louisiana Department of Health regulates medical marijuana. A patient with a recommendation from an authorized clinician buys from licensed retailers, and raw flower is limited to 71 grams (2.5 ounces) every 14 days. State law exempts patients in the program from the possession penalties.
medical.citation: Louisiana Department of Health; La. R.S. 40:966(F)

adult-use.detail: You must be 21 or older to buy or grow adult-use marijuana. Adults may carry up to 2 ounces and keep up to 10 ounces at home.
adult-use.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

buying.detail: Licensed marijuana establishments sell to adults. Visitors from other states must be 21 or older and show a valid government-issued ID.
buying.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

driving.detail: It is illegal to drive under the influence of cannabis or to have an open container of marijuana in the passenger area of a car.
driving.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

employment.short: Medical patients, under a court ruling
employment.detail: The Cannabis Control Commission tells people to check the rules where they work: employers may have their own policies on marijuana use. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists a protection for medical patients through a court ruling: the state’s high court held that the anti-discrimination law covers disabled employees who use medical cannabis, so an employer must consider a reasonable accommodation unless it would be an undue hardship (Barbuto v. Advantage Sales and Marketing); that part is not yet checked against an official source.
employment.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws; Barbuto v. Advantage Sales and Marketing and G.L. c. 151B, § 4, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.detail: Adults may grow up to six plants for personal use, and up to 12 plants when two or more adults live in the home.
home-grow.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

medical.detail: The Medical Use of Marijuana Program serves registered patients and caregivers. Out-of-state residents cannot buy medical marijuana in Massachusetts.
medical.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission

possession.detail: Adults may carry up to 2 ounces and possess up to 10 ounces at home.
possession.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

public-use.detail: Cannabis cannot be used in any form in public places or on federal land.
public-use.citation: Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission, Know the laws

record-relief.short: Amounts that have since been decriminalized
record-relief.detail: Massachusetts’s courts say a person can ask a judge to expunge, meaning permanently destroy, the court records of marijuana offenses where the amount involved has since been decriminalized (G.L. c. 276, § 100K¼, in effect since November 9, 2022). The petitioner must show the amount was two ounces or less, ten ounces or less inside a primary residence, or six or fewer plants for personal use or twelve or fewer on the premises. The petition is filed with the clerk of the court that heard the case, with a copy to the District Attorney, and the court is to act within 30 days. Separately, the Governor’s pardon forgives state convictions for simple possession before March 13, 2024; the courts’ law library says most people need not act and may request a pardon certificate.
record-relief.citation: G.L. c. 276, § 100K¼, per the Massachusetts Trial Court’s petition form (11/22) and the Trial Court Law Libraries’ criminal records page

sharing.detail: Adults may give away up to 2 ounces of marijuana, or the equivalent in products set by the Cannabis Control Commission, to another adult 21 or older without payment, as long as it is not advertised or promoted. The 2-ounce limit took effect April 19, 2026.
sharing.citation: M.G.L. c. 94G, § 7(a)(4), as amended by Acts 2026, c. 65

adult-use.detail: The Maryland Cannabis Administration states that cannabis is legal for adults 21 and older.
adult-use.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, BeCannabisSmart

buying.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy from a licensed dispensary after showing government-issued photo ID, up to the personal use amount.
buying.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs

driving.detail: It is illegal to smoke or use cannabis while driving. Driving while impaired by cannabis carries the same penalties as driving drunk.
driving.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, BeCannabisSmart guide (October 2025)

employment.short: Fire and rescue workers who are patients
employment.detail: The Maryland Cannabis Administration says the Cannabis Reform Act does not address cannabis use or impairment in the workplace, or employer drug screening: people remain subject to existing laws and to workplace policies, including policies that ban cannabis use. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists one protection, for fire and rescue employees who are certified medical cannabis patients (Md. Code, State Gov’t § 20-606); that part is not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs; Md. Code, State Gov’t § 20-606, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to two plants at home, out of public view. A household may have no more than two, however many adults live there.
home-grow.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs

medical.detail: The Maryland Cannabis Administration runs a medical cannabis program alongside adult use.
medical.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration

possession.short: 1.5 oz flower, 12 g concentrate, 750 mg THC
possession.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 1.5 ounces of flower, 12 grams of concentrated cannabis, or products with up to 750 milligrams of THC. This is the personal use amount.
possession.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs

public-use.detail: Smoking cannabis is prohibited in all indoor and outdoor public spaces, including parks, event venues, bars, restaurants, streets and sidewalks.
public-use.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, BeCannabisSmart guide (October 2025)

record-relief.short: Cases where possession was the only charge
record-relief.detail: The Maryland Cannabis Administration says the 2022 and 2023 laws set up a process to expunge cases in which possession of less than 10 grams of cannabis is the only charge, and include other expungement provisions. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists that expungement as automatic and due by July 2024, says the state appears to have missed the deadline, and notes that the governor’s June 2024 pardons do not themselves expunge a record; those points are not yet checked against the state’s own law.
record-relief.citation: Maryland Cannabis Administration, Adult-use cannabis FAQs; Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

sharing.detail: Adults 21 and older may share up to the personal use amount with each other without payment. Gifts tied to another transaction, or offered with a sale of goods or services, do not count.
sharing.citation: Maryland Department of Legislative Services, HB 441 fiscal and policy note (2024), current law

adult-use.detail: Maine’s adult use program serves consumers 21 and older, who may possess up to 2.5 ounces.
adult-use.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

buying.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy up to 2.5 ounces from a licensed cannabis store, no more than 10 grams of it concentrate.

driving.short: OUI applies; no use in vehicles
driving.detail: Driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal and can bring an OUI charge. The driver and passengers may not consume cannabis in a vehicle on a public way.
driving.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions; 28-B M.R.S. § 1501(2)(B)

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Maine as barring an employer from refusing to employ or otherwise penalizing a person solely for being a qualifying patient or caregiver, unless that would violate federal law or cost a federal contract or funding. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: 22 M.R.S. § 2430-C(3), per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.detail: Each resident 21 or older may grow up to six mature plants, 12 immature plants and an unlimited number of seedlings.
home-grow.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

medical.detail: Maine runs both a medical cannabis program and an adult use program.
medical.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

possession.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 2.5 ounces, of which up to 10 grams may be concentrate.
possession.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

public-use.detail: Use in any form is prohibited in public places. Neither the driver nor passengers may consume cannabis in a vehicle on a public way.
public-use.citation: Maine Office of Cannabis Policy, Frequently asked questions

record-relief.detail: Maine’s courts say sealing is not automatic: a person files a Motion to Seal Criminal History (form CR-218) with the clerk of the court where the conviction occurred, and the court holds a hearing. Eligible marijuana convictions are certain Class D possession and cultivation crimes, listed by statute section on the courts’ page, committed before January 30, 2017. At least four years must have passed since the sentence was fully completed, with no later convictions and no pending charges. A sealed record is not erased, since Maine has no expungement, but it is not disclosed to employers, landlords, lenders or school admissions officers, and the person may answer most inquiries as if the conviction had not occurred; criminal justice agencies and the courts can still see it.
record-relief.citation: 15 M.R.S. §§ 2263 to 2265, per the State of Maine Judicial Branch’s Sealing Your Criminal Record page

sharing.detail: Adults may transfer up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 10 grams of it concentrate, to another adult 21 or older without remuneration. Remuneration includes a donation or other payment received as part of the transfer.

adult-use.detail: Michigan law allows personal possession and use of marijuana by people 21 and older.
adult-use.citation: Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, Consumer connection

buying.detail: Licensed marijuana retailers may sell to adults 21 and older. Adults may purchase and possess up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 15 grams of it concentrate.

driving.detail: The adult-use law does not authorize operating a vehicle or other machinery under the influence of marijuana.
driving.citation: Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act

employment.short: Employers may enforce workplace drug policies
employment.detail: Michigan’s adult-use law says it does not require an employer to permit or accommodate conduct the act allows in any workplace or on the employer’s property. It does not prevent an employer from refusing to hire, discharging or disciplining a person for violating a workplace drug policy or for working while under the influence of marihuana.

home-grow.detail: Adults may grow up to 12 plants for personal use within their residence, with no more than 12 plants on the premises at once.

medical.detail: The Michigan Medical Marijuana Program registers patients and caregivers.
medical.citation: Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, Consumer connection

possession.short: 2.5 oz (15 g concentrate); 10 oz at home
possession.detail: Adults may possess up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 15 grams of it concentrate. Within their residence they may keep up to 10 ounces, plus marijuana from plants grown there.

public-use.detail: The adult-use law does not authorize consuming marijuana in public.
public-use.citation: Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act

record-relief.short: Clean Slate after 7 years; marijuana by application
record-relief.detail: Michigan’s Attorney General says the State Police run a daily automatic process under the Clean Slate laws, which cover criminal records in general and are not specific to cannabis: misdemeanors can be set aside after seven years (any number punishable by less than 93 days, up to four of 93 days or more) and up to two felonies after ten years, with no application. Separately, under MCL 780.621e a person convicted of a misdemeanor marijuana offense (possession, use, selling paraphernalia or a matching local ordinance) may apply to the convicting court on form MC 227a; the conduct is presumed to be something that would not have been a crime on or after December 6, 2018, and if the prosecutor does not answer within 60 days the court must set the conviction aside. A set-aside removes the conviction from public view; law enforcement and some licensing agencies may still see it.
record-relief.citation: MCL 780.621e and 780.621g, per the State Court Administrative Office’s Clean Slate overview and the Department of Attorney General’s Expungement Assistance page

sharing.detail: Adults may give away up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 15 grams of it concentrate, to another adult 21 or older without payment, as long as the transfer is not advertised or promoted.

adult-use.detail: A person 21 or older may possess up to 2 ounces of flower in public and 2 pounds at home, plus 8 grams of concentrate and edibles with up to 800 milligrams of THC in total.
adult-use.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

buying.detail: Adult-use cannabis is available for purchase at any licensed adult-use retailer.
buying.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Guide to Safer Cannabis Use (June 2026)

driving.detail: Driving under the influence of cannabis is illegal and subject to additional DWI sanctions.
driving.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

employment.detail: An employer may not refuse to hire an applicant, or discipline or discharge an employee, for using lawful consumable products off the employer’s premises during nonworking hours. Cannabis flower, cannabis products and lower-potency hemp edibles count as lawful products under Minnesota law. Employers may still act on use, possession or impairment during working hours, on work premises or while operating the employer’s vehicle or equipment, or where federal or state law requires it or a federal benefit would be lost. Exceptions include bona fide occupational requirements and conflicts of interest.
employment.citation: Minn. Stat. § 181.938

home-grow.short: Up to 8 plants per home, 4 mature
home-grow.detail: Plants must be kept in an enclosed, locked space that is not open to public view.
home-grow.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

medical.detail: The Office of Cannabis Management runs Minnesota’s medical cannabis program.
medical.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management

possession.short: 2 ounces in public, 2 pounds at home
possession.detail: Also 8 grams of concentrate and edibles infused with a combined 800 milligrams of THC or less.
possession.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

public-use.detail: Use and possession are banned at public and charter schools, state correctional facilities, federal property, federally subsidized housing and an employer’s premises, and while driving or operating heavy machinery.
public-use.citation: Minnesota Office of Cannabis Management, Adult-use cannabis

record-relief.short: Certain misdemeanors; a board reviews felonies
record-relief.detail: Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension says the Adult-Use Cannabis Act requires automatic expungement of certain earlier cannabis records; it expunged the qualifying records in its system in May 2024 and will review again in 2026. The state’s cannabis record site says these are misdemeanor convictions and certain offenses that did not end in a conviction, that sealed records will not show on most background checks, and that no one is notified: a person can check the courts’ online case search or a courthouse terminal. Felony and gross misdemeanor records go to the Cannabis Expungement Board for review; no application is needed, though a person may apply for earlier consideration. The separate Clean Slate Act, in effect since January 1, 2025, automatically seals certain other records.
record-relief.citation: Minn. Stat. §§ 609A.055 and 609A.06, per the Bureau of Criminal Apprehension’s Expungements page and the state’s cannabis record FAQs

sharing.short: 2 oz flower, 8 g concentrate, 800 mg, free
sharing.detail: Adults may give, for no remuneration, up to 2 ounces of flower, 8 grams of concentrate, or an edible with up to 800 milligrams of THC to another adult 21 or older.

adult-use.detail: Consumers at least 21 years old may possess up to 3 ounces of marijuana.
adult-use.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs

buying.detail: Consumers must show a valid government-issued photo ID to buy adult-use products at a dispensary.
buying.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs

driving.detail: The adult-use section of the constitution does not allow operating a vehicle under the influence of marijuana, consuming it while operating one, or smoking it in a vehicle that is being operated. A conviction requires evidence that the driver was in fact under the influence, not just THC or its metabolites in the system.
driving.citation: Missouri Constitution, Article XIV, Section 2

employment.detail: Missouri’s Department of Health and Senior Services says Article XIV of the state constitution, sections 1 and 2, provides certain employment-related protections for patients and consumers, and that employment questions are outside its authority. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists the patient protections as covering lawful use off the premises in nonworking hours and positive drug tests, with exceptions for impairment at work, loss of a federal benefit and jobs where use affects performance or safety; that part, and what the constitution gives adult consumers, is not yet checked against the state’s own text.
employment.citation: Mo. Const. art. XIV, §§ 1 and 2, per the Department of Health and Senior Services’ FAQ; Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.short: With a state card; 6 flowering plants
home-grow.detail: Consumers need a personal cultivation identification card, valid for 12 months and renewable. A cardholder may grow six flowering plants, six nonflowering plants over 14 inches and six under 14 inches, 18 in all. Flowering plants must be labeled with the consumer’s name. The plants, and any harvest beyond 3 ounces, must be kept in an enclosed, locked facility at a private residence.
home-grow.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs; Cannabis cultivation fact sheet

medical.detail: Missouri issues medical marijuana ID cards to patients.
medical.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Cannabis regulation

possession.detail: Consumers may possess up to 3 ounces at any time.
possession.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs

public-use.detail: The constitution does not allow consuming marijuana in a public place outside a licensed area, or smoking it where tobacco smoking is prohibited.
public-use.citation: Missouri Constitution, Article XIV, Section 2

record-relief.short: Offenses that are no longer crimes
record-relief.detail: Missouri’s Department of Health and Senior Services says the law lets people with certain non-violent marijuana offenses petition for release from incarceration, parole or probation and to have their records expunged, and that sales-tax revenue pays the government bodies that carry out expungement of certain marijuana offenses. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Amendment 3 as directing courts to expunge offenses that are no longer crimes without a petition, misdemeanors by June 8, 2023 and felonies by December 8, 2023; that part is not yet checked against the state’s own text.
record-relief.citation: Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, Adult use FAQs; Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

sharing.detail: Adults may deliver or distribute up to 3 ounces of dried, unprocessed marijuana, or its equivalent, without consideration. Giving marijuana to anyone under 21 is not allowed.

adult-use.detail: Mississippi has no adult-use law. The state Health Department’s medical cannabis program says recreational use and possession remain illegal. Its patient toolkit lists a $250 fine for a first offense of up to 30 grams outside the program, jail time for repeat offenses, and a felony for more than 30 grams.
adult-use.citation: Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program toolkit: patient rights and applicable laws (2026)

employment.short: Employers need not permit medical cannabis use
employment.detail: Mississippi’s Medical Cannabis Program says the law does not require employers to permit medical cannabis use or to exempt employees from drug testing.
employment.citation: Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program, Patient Rights & Applicable Laws (program toolkit)

medical.detail: The Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program accepts applications from patients, caregivers, medical practitioners, facilities and services.
medical.citation: Mississippi Medical Cannabis Program

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older with ID may buy from licensed dispensaries in counties where adult sales are allowed (green counties). Possession limits are 1 ounce of flower, 8 grams of concentrate and 800 milligrams of THC in products. Using marijuana in a public place is prohibited.
adult-use.citation: Montana Department of Revenue, adult-use consumer summary

buying.detail: Adults 21 and older with ID may buy from licensed dispensaries in counties where adult sales are allowed (green counties).
buying.citation: Montana Department of Revenue, adult-use consumer summary

driving.detail: State law does not permit operating a vehicle under the influence of marijuana, consuming it while operating a vehicle, or smoking or consuming it in the passenger seat of an enclosed vehicle while it is being operated.

employment.detail: Marijuana is a lawful product under Montana’s lawful-product law. An employer may not refuse to employ someone, or discriminate in pay, promotion or other terms of employment, because the person legally uses a lawful product off the employer’s premises during nonworking hours. The rule does not apply to use that affects job performance or the safety of other employees, or that conflicts with a bona fide occupational qualification. An employer also does not violate it by acting in the belief that an established substance abuse or alcohol policy, a professional contract or a collective bargaining agreement permits the action.

home-grow.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to two mature plants and two seedlings at a private residence, and no more than twice that at one residence. Plants, and any harvest over 1 ounce, must be kept in a locked space out of public view, and a grower who does not own the home needs the owner’s written permission. The Department of Revenue describes home growing as open to Montana residents.
home-grow.citation: MCA 16-12-106(1)(c); Montana Department of Revenue, Know before you grow

medical.detail: Montana residents with a Montana physician’s recommendation can get a one-year registry card for $20 and buy up to 1 ounce a day and 5 ounces a month at any licensed dispensary.
medical.citation: Montana Department of Revenue, cardholder information

possession.short: 1 oz flower, 8 g concentrate, 800 mg THC
possession.detail: Possession limits are 1 ounce of flower, 8 grams of concentrate and 800 milligrams of THC in products.
possession.citation: Montana Department of Revenue, adult-use consumer summary

public-use.detail: State law does not permit consuming marijuana in a public place, except as allowed by the department, or on public transportation. Smoking it in a public place can bring a civil fine of up to $50.
public-use.citation: MCA 16-12-108(1)(k) and 16-12-106(4); Montana Department of Revenue, adult-use consumer summary

record-relief.short: Acts the marijuana law now permits
record-relief.detail: A person who has completed a sentence for an act that Montana’s marijuana law now permits, or punishes less severely, may petition the sentencing court to expunge the conviction or to redesignate it as a misdemeanor or civil infraction. The court presumes the person qualifies unless the county attorney gives a reasonable basis otherwise, and no hearing is needed unless the person asks for one. A person still serving a sentence may petition for expungement or resentencing. Filing does not affect a person’s separate right to petition for misdemeanor expungement.

sharing.detail: Adults may transfer up to 1 ounce of usable marijuana to another adult 21 or older, or to a registered cardholder, without consideration. No more than 8 grams may be concentrate and no more than 800 milligrams of THC may be in solid edibles.

adult-use.detail: North Carolina has no adult-use law. Possessing half an ounce or less is a Class 3 misdemeanor. More than half an ounce, up to 1.5 ounces, is a Class 1 misdemeanor, and more than 1.5 ounces is a Class I felony.
adult-use.citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. 90-95(d)(4)

medical.detail: State law lets a caregiver possess and give hemp extract with less than 0.9% THC and at least 5% CBD to a person with intractable epilepsy, with a certificate of analysis for the extract.
medical.citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. 90-94.1

adult-use.detail: North Dakota has no adult-use law. Without a medical card, possessing less than half an ounce is an infraction. Half an ounce up to 500 grams is a class B misdemeanor, and more than 500 grams is a class A misdemeanor.

medical.short: Yes, with a state registry card
medical.detail: North Dakota residents with written certification from a North Dakota-licensed provider can apply for a registry card ($40). Cardholders may buy only from the state’s eight registered dispensaries; state law does not protect marijuana bought anywhere else.
medical.citation: North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services, Medical Marijuana Patients

adult-use.detail: Nebraska has no adult-use law. Without a medical recommendation, a first offense for 1 ounce or less is an infraction with a citation and a $300 fine, and a drug education course may be required. More than 1 ounce, up to 1 pound, is a Class III misdemeanor.
adult-use.citation: Neb. Rev. Stat. 28-416

medical.detail: Voters approved Initiative 437 in 2024. It lets a qualified patient with a health care practitioner’s written recommendation use and possess up to 5 ounces of cannabis. The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission regulates the program; its application page says only cultivator and manufacturer license applications have opened so far.
medical.citation: Neb. Rev. Stat. 71-24,104; Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission

adult-use.detail: New Hampshire has no adult-use law. Since 2017, possessing three-quarters of an ounce of marijuana or less has been a violation, not a crime, for people 18 and older; possessing more is a misdemeanor. That is how the Attorney General’s office described the law in a 2019 court brief; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: RSA 318-B:2-c and 318-B:26, II(c), per the State’s brief in case No. 2018-0647 (2019); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

employment.short: Medical patients, under a court ruling
employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists New Hampshire as protecting medical patients through a court ruling, not the therapeutic cannabis law: the state Supreme Court held in 2022 that therapeutic cannabis use may call for a reasonable accommodation under the Law Against Discrimination. Its chart notes the therapeutic cannabis law does not require accommodating use on an employer’s premises. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: Paine v. Ride-Away (N.H. 2022); RSA 354-A; RSA 126-X:3, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

medical.detail: The Therapeutic Cannabis Program issues registry ID cards that let cardholders buy from Alternative Treatment Centers.
medical.citation: New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services, Therapeutic Cannabis Program

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older may have up to 6 ounces of cannabis.
adult-use.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

buying.detail: Buy at the New Jersey licensed dispensaries listed in the state’s dispensary finder.
buying.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

driving.detail: The state’s impaired-driving laws apply to driving under the influence of cannabis.
driving.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

employment.short: Cannabis use alone cannot decide hiring or firing
employment.detail: The Cannabis Regulatory Commission says general cannabis use cannot be a determining factor in hiring or firing someone, and that an employer may not take adverse action solely because a drug test finds cannabinoid metabolites from lawful use. Employers may keep a drug- and alcohol-free workplace and may require a drug test on reasonable suspicion of use at work, on signs of impairment, in a random testing program or after a workplace accident. A positive test together with documented signs of impairment during work hours may support action. Employers bound by a federal contract may follow federal rules.
employment.citation: N.J.S.A. 24:6I-52, per the Cannabis Regulatory Commission’s workplace page and guidance (September 9, 2022)

home-grow.detail: New Jersey law does not allow personal growing.
home-grow.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Legal cannabis in New Jersey (September 2025)

medical.detail: New Jersey runs a Medicinal Cannabis Program for patients.
medical.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission

possession.detail: Adults 21 and older may have up to 6 ounces.
possession.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

public-use.detail: Cannabis smoking is allowed where cigarette smoking is permitted unless stated otherwise, and landlords may prohibit use. Licensed consumption areas admit only people 21 and older with photo ID.
public-use.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

record-relief.detail: The New Jersey Judiciary says it expunges eligible marijuana and hashish cases automatically, with no request needed, under the Marijuana Decriminalization Law; by February 2022 it had cleared more than 362,000 cases. An expunged case leaves the public court record and need not be reported on applications for jobs, housing or college. A person who believes a case should have qualified can file a motion for judicial review, and can get a certification of expungement from the court that heard the case or the Superior Court Clerk’s Office in Trenton.
record-relief.citation: New Jersey Judiciary, Marijuana Record Expungement (February 1, 2022)

sharing.detail: Adults may give up to 28.35 grams (1 ounce) to another adult 21 or older and may not accept any payment or compensation for it.
sharing.citation: New Jersey Cannabis Regulatory Commission, Recreational cannabis in New Jersey

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older may cultivate, buy, possess and consume cannabis.
adult-use.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis in New Mexico

buying.detail: The first licensed adult-use sales began on April 1, 2022.
buying.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis in New Mexico

driving.detail: The state’s cannabis FAQ says using cannabis or cannabis products while driving is illegal.
driving.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis FAQs

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists New Mexico as barring employers from taking adverse action against an applicant or employee for conduct its medical cannabis law allows. Its chart lists exceptions for federal law or loss of a federal benefit, and for jobs the employer deems safety-sensitive. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: N.M. Stat. § 26-2B-9, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.short: 12 plants per adult, 6 mature; 12 mature per home
home-grow.detail: An adult 21 or older may grow up to 12 plants at a private residence, no more than six of them mature. A household with several adults may have no more than 12 mature plants.
home-grow.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Personal use of cannabis

medical.detail: The Department of Health continues to oversee the medical cannabis patient program.
medical.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis in New Mexico

possession.short: 2 oz, 16 g extract, 800 mg edibles in public
possession.detail: Outside their home, adults may have up to 2 ounces of cannabis, 16 grams of extract and 800 milligrams of edibles. More may be kept at home if it is not visible from a public place.

public-use.short: No; private homes or licensed lounges
public-use.detail: Consumption must take place at a private residence or a licensed consumption lounge. Using cannabis in public spaces such as restaurants, parks and sidewalks can bring a fine of up to $50.
public-use.citation: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Cannabis FAQs

record-relief.detail: New Mexico’s Regulation and Licensing Department says the Criminal Records Expungement Act, in effect since January 1, 2020, lets a qualifying person petition a court to expunge certain criminal records, including marijuana-related records, and points to the state courts’ expungement page. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists a separate law that reviews and expunges convictions for legalized conduct automatically, limited since 2023 to cannabis convictions that stand alone; that part is not yet checked against the state’s own law.
record-relief.citation: NMSA 1978, §§ 29-3A-1 to 29-3A-9, per the Regulation and Licensing Department’s FAQs; Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

sharing.detail: Adults may transfer cannabis to another adult 21 or older without financial consideration, up to the amount lawfully purchased and obtained under state law.

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older can legally possess up to 2.5 ounces of cannabis and up to 1/4 ounce of concentrate.
adult-use.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

buying.detail: Adults may buy cannabis only from state-licensed retail stores and must show ID proving they are 21 or older.
buying.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

driving.detail: It is illegal to drive under the influence of cannabis.
driving.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

employment.detail: It is unlawful for a Nevada employer to refuse to hire a prospective employee because a screening test shows marijuana. That does not cover applicants to be firefighters or emergency medical technicians, jobs that require driving and for which law requires screening tests, or jobs the employer determines could adversely affect the safety of others. It gives way to an employment contract or collective bargaining agreement and to federal law, and does not cover positions funded by a federal grant. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists no protection for current employees’ adult use, and lists a duty to try to reasonably accommodate medical cardholders’ use away from work (NRS 678C.850); those two points are not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: NRS 613.132; Marijuana Policy Project’s table and chart for the other points

home-grow.short: Only if no store within 25 miles
home-grow.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to six plants each and 12 per household, but only if no state-licensed retail cannabis store is within 25 miles of the home.
home-grow.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

medical.detail: The Cannabis Compliance Board oversees medical cannabis, including patient ID cards.
medical.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board

possession.detail: Adults 21 and older can legally possess up to 2.5 ounces of cannabis and up to 1/4 ounce of concentrated cannabis.
possession.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

public-use.detail: Cannabis cannot be used in any public place, or in a moving vehicle even as a passenger.
public-use.citation: Nevada Cannabis Compliance Board, Laws and regulations

record-relief.detail: Nevada law lets a person convicted of an offense that was later decriminalized, by an act of the Legislature or a voter initiative, send a written request to any court where they were convicted to seal the records of that conviction held by the court and by criminal justice agencies. No court or agency may charge a fee. The court notifies the prosecutor, who has 10 judicial days to object in writing; with no objection the court must grant the request, and after an objection it holds a hearing and grants the request unless the prosecutor shows good cause by clear and convincing evidence. The section covers decriminalized offenses in general and does not name marijuana; it does not apply to traffic offenses.
record-relief.citation: NRS 179.271 (Nevada Revised Statutes, revised April 15, 2026)

sharing.short: Up to 2.5 oz or 1/4 oz concentrate, free
sharing.detail: An adult may deliver up to 2.5 ounces of usable cannabis or 1/4 ounce of concentrated cannabis to another adult 21 or older without remuneration, if the delivery is not advertised or promoted.

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess, buy and transport up to 3 ounces of cannabis and 24 grams of concentrate. Up to 5 pounds may be kept at home if secured from anyone under 21.
adult-use.citation: N.Y. Penal Law §§ 222.05 and 222.15; Office of Cannabis Management

buying.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy up to 3 ounces of cannabis and 24 grams of concentrate.
buying.citation: N.Y. Penal Law § 222.05; Office of Cannabis Management

driving.detail: Driving impaired by a drug is treated like alcohol-impaired driving. Cannabis in a vehicle must be in a closed container, and smoking cannabis in a vehicle is illegal for drivers and passengers.
driving.citation: N.Y. Vehicle and Traffic Law § 1192; Office of Cannabis Management

employment.detail: Employers generally may not act against workers for lawful off-duty cannabis use away from the workplace and without employer property. Employers may still act when required by state or federal law, when a worker shows specific articulable signs of impairment on the job, or when allowing it would violate federal law or risk a federal contract or funding.
employment.citation: N.Y. Labor Law § 201-d

home-grow.short: 3 mature and 3 immature plants per adult
home-grow.detail: No more than six mature and six immature plants per residence, only at a private residence and secured from anyone under 21. Localities may regulate but not effectively ban home growing.
home-grow.citation: N.Y. Penal Law § 222.15; Office of Cannabis Management, Home cultivation FAQs

medical.detail: A certifying provider may certify a patient for any condition they judge suitable. Patients or caregivers may buy up to a 60-day supply. A 2025 law (S3294A) lets registered patients and caregivers 18 and older grow at home and lets patients certified in other states buy in New York.
medical.citation: Office of Cannabis Management, Patients; Senate Bill S3294A (2025)

possession.short: 3 ounces and 24 g concentrate; 5 pounds at home
possession.detail: Up to 5 pounds may be kept at home if secured from anyone under 21.
possession.citation: N.Y. Penal Law §§ 222.05 and 222.15

public-use.short: Where tobacco smoking is allowed, with exceptions
public-use.detail: Not in a motor vehicle, where smoking or vaping is banned, on school grounds or buses, or on federal property. Breaking these limits carries a civil penalty of up to $25 or up to 20 hours of community service.
public-use.citation: N.Y. Penal Law § 222.10; Office of Cannabis Management

record-relief.detail: Convictions under the listed marijuana offenses (possession up to 16 ounces or sale up to 25 grams) are expunged automatically, with no motion or fee and no notice sent. Expunged cases do not appear on background checks and need not be disclosed. Other marijuana convictions require a CPL 440.46-a motion. Separately, the Clean Slate Act, in effect since November 16, 2024, provides automatic sealing of eligible convictions for certain civil background checks; courts have until November 16, 2027 to finish setting it up. Sex crimes and non-drug Class A felonies are not eligible.
record-relief.citation: N.Y. Unified Court System: cannabis expungement page and Clean Slate Act page

sharing.detail: Adults may give up to 3 ounces and 24 grams of concentrate to another adult 21 or older without compensation. “Gifting” tied to a sale is not lawful sharing.

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older may use and possess marijuana bought from a licensed Ohio dispensary, up to 2.5 ounces of plant material and 15 grams of extract in total, counting homegrown marijuana.
adult-use.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221

buying.detail: Adult-use marijuana must be bought from a licensed Ohio dispensary.
buying.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221

driving.detail: Neither the adult-use nor the medical law allows driving under the influence. Driving with marijuana or its metabolite at or above set blood or urine concentrations is an offense even without shown impairment, and medical registration is not a defense.
driving.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221 and 4511.19

employment.short: Employers may act on marijuana use
employment.detail: Ohio’s marijuana law does not require employers to allow or accommodate marijuana use, possession or distribution. Employers may refuse to hire, discharge or discipline someone because of marijuana use, and may keep drug-testing, drug-free workplace and zero-tolerance policies. This applies to medical and adult-use marijuana alike.
employment.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.28

home-grow.detail: Subject to secured-area, primary-residence and other statutory conditions.
home-grow.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.04

medical.detail: A patient registered with the Division of Cannabis Control, with a certified physician’s recommendation for a qualifying condition, may possess up to a 90-day supply bought from a licensed dispensary. Caregivers register separately.
medical.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.22 and 3796.08

possession.detail: The limit counts dispensary and homegrown marijuana together.
possession.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.221

public-use.detail: Using adult-use or homegrown marijuana in a public place is prohibited. Use is legal at a private residence, subject to the property owner’s rules.
public-use.citation: Ohio Revised Code 3796.04

record-relief.detail: An application-based process to expunge specified marijuana and hashish possession cases from before March 20, 2026. Eligibility and court procedures are stated in the statute.
record-relief.citation: Ohio Revised Code 2953.321

sharing.short: Same amounts, free, on private property only
sharing.detail: An adult may give the same amounts to another adult in a single day, without payment, only on private residential or agricultural property. Other transfers require a license.

adult-use.detail: Oklahoma has no adult-use law. In March 2023, more than 61% of voters rejected State Question 820, which would have legalized recreational marijuana. National compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: Oklahoma State Senate (2023); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Oklahoma as barring employers from penalizing an applicant or employee solely for being a medical marijuana licensee or for a positive marijuana test. Its chart lists exceptions for federal law or funding, no valid license, use or impairment at work and safety-sensitive jobs. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: 63 O.S. § 427.8, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

medical.detail: The Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority regulates the state’s medical marijuana program.
medical.citation: Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older can possess and use cannabis within set limits.
adult-use.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

buying.detail: Marijuana items may be bought at an OLCC-licensed retail location. A customer may buy up to 2 ounces of usable marijuana at one time or in one day.
buying.citation: Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission, Frequently asked questions

driving.detail: Driving while impaired, including by cannabis, remains illegal.
driving.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

employment.detail: The Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission says the state’s cannabis law does not change existing employment law. Employers who test for drugs may keep doing so, and whether a person can be fired for using marijuana depends on the employer’s policies.
employment.citation: Oregon Liquor and Cannabis Commission, Frequently asked questions

home-grow.detail: The personal possession limits include four marijuana plants.
home-grow.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

medical.detail: The Oregon Medical Marijuana Act allows medical use for qualifying medical conditions.
medical.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

possession.detail: Also 16 ounces of solid products or concentrates, 72 ounces of liquid products and 1 ounce of extracts bought from a marijuana retailer.
possession.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

public-use.detail: Public use remains illegal.
public-use.citation: Oregon Health Authority, Cannabis laws in Oregon

record-relief.short: Qualifying convictions, no fee or waiting period
record-relief.detail: Oregon’s courts say ORS 475C.397 requires a court to set aside a qualifying marijuana conviction, with no waiting period and no filing fee, unless the prosecutor objects within 30 days that the conviction does not qualify. On the statewide form a person declares that the conduct took place before July 1, 2015 and that the conviction was for conduct described in ORS 475C.305 or for possessing less than one ounce of dried marijuana. The same form asks the court under ORS 137.222 to lower a conviction for an offense that has since been reduced. A set-aside seals the record and the person is treated as not previously convicted. Separately, on November 21, 2022 the Governor pardoned state-court convictions for possessing one ounce or less in pre-2015 cases where the person was 21 or older, it was the only charge and there was no victim; those records were sealed without an application.
record-relief.citation: ORS 475C.397 and ORS 137.222, per the Oregon Judicial Department’s marijuana set-aside motion form (July 2023)
