sharing.detail: An adult may deliver up to 1 ounce of usable marijuana at a time to another adult 21 or older for noncommercial purposes.

adult-use.detail: Pennsylvania has no adult-use law. Without a medical card, possessing up to 30 grams of marijuana or 8 grams of hashish is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 30 days in jail, a fine of up to $500, or both.
adult-use.citation: Controlled Substance, Drug, Device and Cosmetic Act (Act 64 of 1972)

driving.short: Any amount in the blood is DUI
driving.detail: Driving with any amount of a Schedule I controlled substance or its metabolite in the blood is DUI, impaired or not. Marijuana is Schedule I under state law, and there is no exception for medical patients.

employment.detail: An employer may not fire, refuse to hire or otherwise discriminate against someone solely because they are certified to use medical marijuana. Employers need not allow use at work and may discipline employees for being under the influence at work when their conduct falls below the standard of care for the job.
employment.citation: Medical Marijuana Act (Act 16 of 2016), section 2103(b)

home-grow.detail: Only grower/processors permitted by the Department of Health may grow medical marijuana. Pennsylvania has no adult-use home-grow law.
home-grow.citation: Medical Marijuana Act (Act 16 of 2016)

medical.detail: Medical use is lawful only for a registered patient or caregiver with a Department of Health ID card and practitioner certification. A dispensary may sell no more than a 90-day supply, and smoking medical marijuana is unlawful.
medical.citation: Medical Marijuana Act (Act 16 of 2016)

record-relief.detail: Clean Slate limits access to (seals) certain records automatically: charges that did not end in a conviction; summary convictions after five years; and second- and third-degree misdemeanors and misdemeanors punishable by up to two years after seven years free of convictions punishable by a year or more. Court-ordered restitution must be paid. A pardon is a separate step. The law covers criminal records in general, not only cannabis cases; whether one record qualifies depends on the full record and the exclusions in the statute.
record-relief.citation: 18 Pa.C.S. § 9122.2, as amended by Act 36 of 2023

adult-use.detail: Adult use has been legal since December 1, 2022 for people at least 21 years old.
adult-use.citation: Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission, Frequently asked questions

buying.detail: Licensed compassion centers are the retail stores currently selling adult-use cannabis.
buying.citation: Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission, Frequently asked questions

driving.detail: The law does not permit operating a vehicle, boat or aircraft under the influence of cannabis. Metabolites in a person’s system do not by themselves mean the person is under the influence.

employment.detail: An employer may not fire or discipline an employee solely for private, lawful cannabis use outside the workplace, as long as the employee has not worked and is not working under the influence. The rule gives way to a collective bargaining agreement that prohibits such use, and to federal contractors that would lose a federal benefit. For jobs that are hazardous, dangerous or essential to public welfare and safety, an employer may bar use in the 24 hours before a shift. Employers may act on a violation of a workplace drug policy or on working under the influence.
employment.citation: R.I. Gen. Laws § 21-28.11-29(d) and (e)

home-grow.detail: Adults 21 and older may grow up to three mature and three immature plants.
home-grow.citation: Rhode Island Department of Health, Cannabis information for adults

medical.detail: The Cannabis Control Commission regulates both adult-use and medical marijuana.
medical.citation: Rhode Island Cannabis Control Commission, Frequently asked questions

possession.detail: Adults 21 and older may carry up to 1 ounce of flower, or the equivalent in concentrate, and keep up to 10 ounces at home.
possession.citation: Rhode Island Department of Health, Cannabis information for adults

public-use.short: No smoking or vaping in public
public-use.detail: State law does not authorize smoking or vaping cannabis in any public place, and both are banned wherever smoking or vaping tobacco is banned.

record-relief.detail: The Rhode Island Judiciary says the Rhode Island Cannabis Act of 2022 requires the courts to expunge eligible cases and charges automatically, at no cost. Under the Supreme Court’s Executive Order 2023-02 that covers criminal convictions for marijuana possession by people 18 and over and civil violations by people 21 and over, and not other marijuana convictions such as selling, delivering or manufacturing. Cases where possession was the only charge were cleared before April 30, 2023; the Judiciary said cases with other charges were on track for July 1, 2024. A person can check the Judiciary’s Public Portal, where an expunged case no longer appears, and can ask the court that heard the case to act sooner by filing a Notice for Expedited Marijuana Possession Expungement.
record-relief.citation: Rhode Island Cannabis Act (2022) and Supreme Court Executive Order 2023-02, per the Rhode Island Judiciary’s release on phase one of marijuana expungement

sharing.detail: Adults may give away up to 1 ounce of cannabis, or the equivalent in concentrate, to another adult 21 or older without payment, as long as the transfer is not advertised or promoted.

adult-use.detail: South Carolina has no adult-use law. A first offense for 1 ounce or less is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 30 days in jail or a fine of $100 to $200. A second or later offense can bring up to a year in jail or a fine of at least $200.

medical.detail: State law excludes from the definition of marijuana a cannabidiol product with no more than 0.9% THC and more than 15% CBD, for a person with severe epilepsy, such as Lennox-Gastaut or Dravet syndrome, who has a written certification from a South Carolina-licensed physician.
medical.citation: S.C. Code 44-53-110 (definition of marijuana)

adult-use.detail: South Dakota has no adult-use law. The state Health Department says any sale or purchase of cannabis outside licensed medical cannabis establishments is illegal. Possessing 2 ounces or less is a Class 1 misdemeanor (up to one year in county jail, a fine of up to $2,000, or both), as Legislative Research Council staff summarized the law in 2021; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: SDCL 22-42-6, per Legislative Research Council staff (2021); South Dakota Department of Health; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists South Dakota as giving registered patients the same rights as people prescribed medication in dealings with an employer and in drug testing. Its chart says the protections yield to federal obligations and that employers may act on a positive test for safety-sensitive jobs. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: SDCL §§ 34-20G-22 and 34-20G-23, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

medical.detail: Patients get a medical cannabis card, and the Department of Health certifies dispensaries.
medical.citation: South Dakota Department of Health, Medical cannabis

adult-use.detail: Tennessee has no adult-use law. The Attorney General’s 2016 opinion describes possessing any amount as a Class A misdemeanor (up to 11 months and 29 days in jail, a fine of up to $2,500, or both), with minimum fines starting at $250. National compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: Tenn. Code Ann. 39-17-418, per Attorney General Opinion 16-40; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

medical.detail: DISA’s national map lists Tennessee as CBD oil only, marked as legislation passed with a future effective date.
medical.citation: DISA national map

adult-use.detail: Texas has no adult-use law. Possessing under 2 ounces of marijuana is a Class B misdemeanor, punishable by jail time and fines. That is how the Senate Research Center described state law in March 2025; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: Tex. Health & Safety Code 481.121, per the Senate Research Center analysis of S.B. 1059 (2025); Ballotpedia; DISA national map

medical.detail: The Department of Public Safety runs the Compassionate Use Program created by the 2015 Texas Compassionate Use Act. DISA’s national map lists Texas as CBD oil only.
medical.citation: Texas Department of Public Safety; DISA national map

adult-use.detail: Utah has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a class B misdemeanor, and a third conviction within seven years is a class A misdemeanor. That is the law as reprinted in a January 2026 House bill; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: Utah Code 58-37-8(2)(d), as reprinted in 2026 H.B. 253; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

employment.short: Public employees who are medical patients
employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Utah as protecting state and local government employees only: their medical cannabis use is treated like a prescribed controlled substance, and a cardholder may not be retaliated against for a failed drug test without evidence of impairment. Its chart lists exceptions tied to federal funding, clearances and licenses. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: Utah Code § 26-61a-111, as cited in the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

medical.detail: Utah’s Center for Medical Cannabis works to give Utahns safe access to medical cannabis, and its site lists pharmacies that serve patients.
medical.citation: Utah Center for Medical Cannabis

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 2 ounces outside their home and generally may use cannabis in private residences.
adult-use.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

buying.detail: Non-medical sales are currently illegal. Retail sales begin July 1, 2027.
buying.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority

driving.short: No impaired driving or use in a vehicle
driving.detail: It is illegal to drive under the influence of marijuana, or to use it while driving or riding as a passenger.
driving.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

employment.detail: Virginia’s Cannabis Control Authority says workplaces and employers may still prohibit cannabis use by their employees and enforce drug testing, and that Virginia law protects some medical cannabis use from employment action, though perhaps not for every medical user. The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists that protection as covering employees who use cannabis oil under a valid written certification, with exceptions for impairment or possession at work, federal law and some defense-industry employers (Va. Code § 40.1-27.4); that part is not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions; Va. Code § 40.1-27.4, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.detail: Four plants per household, not per person, under specified requirements.
home-grow.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

medical.detail: Virginia runs a medical cannabis program.
medical.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority

possession.detail: Adults 21 and older may possess up to 2 ounces outside their private residence.
possession.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

public-use.detail: Consuming cannabis in any public place is illegal, as is using it while driving or riding as a passenger.
public-use.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

record-relief.detail: Virginia State Police say statutes taking effect July 1, 2026 (Va. Code § 19.2-392.5 and following) seal possession of marijuana offenses, criminal and civil, automatically, along with some other records; the courts’ July 2026 guide refers to former § 18.2-250.1 possession cases as automatically sealed under § 19.2-392.6:1. A no-fee court petition covers records that should have been sealed automatically but were not, offenses the system cannot identify, such as possession of marijuana-related drug paraphernalia, and misdemeanor sale or distribution of marijuana with an offense date on or after January 1, 1986. Other convictions can be sealed by petition after seven years for a misdemeanor or ten for a felony, with further conditions. Background check companies may not share sealed records.
record-relief.citation: Va. Code § 19.2-392.5 and following, per the Virginia State Police’s Sealing of Criminal Records page and the courts’ sealing guide CC-1203 INST (07/26)

sharing.detail: Adults 21 and older may transfer 2 ounces or less to another adult without payment. Gifts tied to a sale or another exchange do not count.
sharing.citation: Virginia Cannabis Control Authority, Frequently asked questions

adult-use.detail: Adults 21 and older with a valid government-issued photo ID may buy cannabis.
adult-use.citation: Vermont Cannabis Control Board, Frequently asked questions

buying.detail: Cannabis may only be bought legally from a licensed retailer or an integrated licensee’s retail arm. Since July 1, 2026, a retailer may sell up to 2 ounces, or the equivalent in products, in a single transaction to a buyer 21 or older with valid photo ID.
buying.citation: Vermont Cannabis Control Board, Frequently asked questions; 7 V.S.A. § 907(b), as amended by Act 176 (2026)

driving.detail: The adult-use law does not protect anyone from arrest or prosecution for operating a vehicle under the influence of cannabis or for consuming cannabis while operating a motor vehicle.

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Vermont as protecting patients through 2018 Attorney General guidance, not the medical cannabis law: a patient with a disability is protected under the state’s Fair Employment Practices Act. Its chart adds that a separate state law restricts drug testing. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: Vermont Attorney General guidance (2018); Fair Employment Practices Act, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

home-grow.detail: Adults may grow up to two mature and four immature plants, and a dwelling unit may have no more than that however many adults live there. Plants must be in an area screened from public view, with access limited to the grower and adults 21 or older who have the grower’s permission.

medical.detail: Vermont has a medical cannabis program.
medical.citation: Vermont Cannabis Control Board

possession.detail: Since July 1, 2026, adults 21 and older may possess up to 2 ounces of cannabis or 10 grams of hashish. Cannabis grown and stored at home under the home-grow rules does not count toward the limit.
possession.citation: 18 V.S.A. § 4230a, as amended by Act 176 (2026)

public-use.detail: Consuming cannabis in any form in a public place is prohibited, with civil penalties of up to $100 for a first offense.
public-use.citation: 7 V.S.A. § 833; Vermont Cannabis Control Board, Public safety and education questions

record-relief.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists Vermont as requiring automatic expungement, by January 1, 2022, of records involving up to two ounces of cannabis, 10 grams of hashish, four mature plants and eight immature plants. Its table says expungement and sealing by petition is available for other offenses after a waiting period. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
record-relief.citation: Marijuana Policy Project’s table of legalization states’ expungement laws

sharing.short: Up to 1 oz or 5 g hashish, not advertised
sharing.detail: An adult 21 or older may dispense up to 1 ounce of cannabis or 5 grams of hashish to another adult 21 or older, as long as it is not advertised or promoted to the public. Unlawful sales are a crime.

adult-use.detail: Only adults 21 and older can buy and possess cannabis.
adult-use.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Know the law

buying.detail: Cannabis can only be sold and bought at state-licensed retail stores, with valid photo ID. Adults may buy up to 1 ounce of usable cannabis, 16 ounces of solid edibles, 72 ounces in liquid form and 7 grams of concentrates.
buying.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Know the law

driving.detail: Driving with more than 5 nanograms of active THC per milliliter of blood is illegal.
driving.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Know the law

employment.detail: Since January 1, 2024, it is unlawful for an employer to discriminate in initial hiring because of a person’s use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace, or because an employer-required drug test finds non-psychoactive cannabis metabolites. The law covers initial hiring only: it does not apply to testing after hiring, such as post-accident or suspicion-based testing, and it leaves drug-free workplace rules in place. It does not cover applicants for jobs that need a federal background investigation or security clearance, jobs with law enforcement agencies and fire departments, other first responders, corrections officers, airline and aerospace jobs, or safety-sensitive jobs the employer identified in advance.

home-grow.detail: Washington does not allow home growing unless you are a qualified medical patient or designated provider with a valid authorization. Growing plants without one is a class C felony; a 2026 bill to allow adult home grows did not pass.
home-grow.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Growing cannabis at home; House bill report on HB 1449 (2025); SB 6204 bill summary

medical.detail: With a health care practitioner’s authorization, an adult patient may grow up to four plants. A recognition card from a medically endorsed store adds tax exemptions and higher limits: by default up to 3 ounces of usable cannabis (or equivalent products) and six plants. Patients 18 to 20 must register to buy.
medical.citation: Washington State Department of Health; RCW 69.51A.210

possession.short: 1 oz, 16 oz solid edibles, 72 oz liquid, 7 g conc.
possession.detail: Adults 21 and older may buy and possess up to 1 ounce of usable cannabis, 16 ounces of solid edibles, 72 ounces of drinks and 7 grams of concentrate.
possession.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Using and having cannabis

public-use.detail: It is illegal to consume cannabis in view of the public.
public-use.citation: Washington State Liquor and Cannabis Board, Know the law

record-relief.detail: Washington’s courts say the law does not vacate a conviction automatically: a person files a petition (form CrRLJ 09.0800) under RCW 9.96.060, gives the prosecutor a copy the same day and attends a hearing. A court will vacate a misdemeanor cannabis conviction if the person was 21 or older at the time of the offense; eligible offenses include those under RCW 69.50.4014 from July 1, 2004, under RCW 69.50.401(e) or (d) from May 21, 1971 to July 1, 2004, and under equivalent local ordinances. After vacation a person may state on job or housing applications that they were never convicted of that crime.
record-relief.citation: RCW 9.96.060, per the Washington Courts’ Instructions for Vacating Misdemeanor and Gross Misdemeanor Convictions (CrRLJ 09.0300, July 2022)

sharing.short: Up to 1/2 oz flower a day, free
sharing.detail: In any 24-hour period, an adult may give another adult 21 or older up to half an ounce of usable cannabis or 8 ounces of solid edibles, with separate limits for other products, with no payment involved. The handoff must take place out of public view in a nonpublic place, or the product must be in its original store packaging.
sharing.citation: RCW 69.50.4013(4), as reprinted in 2026 Senate Bill 6204; House bill report on HB 1449 (2025)

adult-use.detail: Wisconsin has no adult-use law. A first conviction for possession is a misdemeanor (a fine of up to $1,000, up to six months in jail, or both), and a repeat conviction is a Class I felony. That is the Legislative Reference Bureau’s December 2023 summary of current law; national compilations list no adult use as of November 2026.
adult-use.citation: Wis. Stat. 961.41(3g)(e), per Legislative Reference Bureau analysis; Ballotpedia; DISA national map

medical.detail: State law lets a person possess a cannabidiol product with a certification from a Wisconsin-licensed physician, issued within the past year, stating that it treats a medical condition.
medical.citation: Wis. Stat. 961.32(2m)

adult-use.detail: West Virginia has no adult-use law. Possessing marijuana is a misdemeanor punishable by 90 days to 6 months in jail, a fine of up to $1,000, or both. A first offense involving less than 15 grams must be handled through conditional discharge, under which completing probation ends the case without a conviction.

employment.detail: The Marijuana Policy Project, an advocacy group, lists West Virginia as barring employers from discharging, refusing to hire or discriminating against a person solely for being certified to use medical cannabis, with an exception for federal law. Not yet checked against the state’s own law.
employment.citation: W. Va. Code § 16A-15-4, per the Marijuana Policy Project’s chart

medical.detail: Patients apply to the Office of Medical Cannabis for a card, and its site lists dispensaries.
medical.citation: West Virginia Office of Medical Cannabis

adult-use.detail: Wyoming has no adult-use law. Possessing up to 3 ounces of marijuana in plant form is a misdemeanor punishable by up to 12 months in jail, a $1,000 fine, or both. Larger amounts are a felony punishable by up to 5 years in prison, a $10,000 fine, or both.

medical.detail: Wyoming law bars practitioners from prescribing or dispensing marijuana or THC except FDA-approved drugs such as dronabinol. Its former article on supervised medical use of hemp extracts (W.S. 35-7-1901 to 35-7-1903) was repealed in 2019, and hemp products are now outside the controlled substances law.
